comments.issue_title: Add `Option.get_help_spec` to extract the help's left part of an hidden option
comments.author: kdeldycke
comments.body:
> Maybe there's a better name for this. Why is this the "spec"? Perhaps, `format_help_names` or something?

I guess `name` is even more confusing, given the whole PR I am trying to land around the real `name` property of `Argument` and `Option` at https://github.com/pallets/click/pull/3827 . I choose `spec` to differentiate it with `name` for that reason. And differentiate it from `decls`.

So the transformation pipeline become:
- `decls`: what the developer provide to its argument or option
- `spec`: what the user see in `--help` and what it provide to the CLI
- `name`: what is used internally in Click to identify that argument or option

If I had full reigns over the Click codebase, I would rename that cursed `name` into `id` or `uid`.

comments.issue_title: `click.edit` on Windows throws WinError 14001 or 87
comments.author: Vaibhavtripathi7
comments.body:
I tried recreating the issue on my own system: `windows 11 build number (26100.9445)`, `python version 3.14`, and also checked for Notepad execution alias toggle which was default nothing to change, but I couldn't recreate it , tested it for for total 30 iterations no failures not even one.
Then I investigated the issue from different paths, and perspectives : first - I tired to crosscheck shlex working and how it is used in the codebase, as `shlex` is based on unix systems, so it treats backslashes differently which can cause an error but as 'notepad' passed directly Nothing could be wrong here( it’s single string so no split), and environment which was passed in click function, was just copy of original one Nothing changed.So that completely eliminated any parsing issue, or conditional check issue as error messages suggested.
So next thing i dig up was, windows error which were mentioned : `INVALID_PARAMETER` and `ERROR_SXS_CANT_GEN_ACTCTX`, I explored few articles on this , one was completely related to this ( it is from Microsoft's own Q&A platform) , and it’s main point was that crash inside a specific alias-resolution dll, is inconsistent or random getting 4 times out of 10 time failures( same condition as described in the this issue description ), but it pointed to alias thing which again i tried to debug and analyse it ( as many users have experience this issue, regarding notepad specifically in windows).
And as i couldn't recreate the error, it is currently too vague to work on a solution and from my conclusion it seems like a know windows platform bug rather than click functionality error, here's is a thread to support this (<https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/2109069/createprocess-on-notepad-exe-fails-due-to-a-crash>) , and as in the thread, someone already tested with full exe path too, but it did not succeed as per them.
I would like to know the maintainers view on this particular issue, and about my findings.

Other path is to tweak the way we call these editors from Click. But it suppose that these editors can be fed with the right options to ask them to wait for us. comments.issue_title: [rejected AI] Fix count=True ignoring non-zero default
comments.author: roli-lpci
comments.body:
`count=True` also accepts string defaults, which Click normally converts through
the option's integer type. On this head, the new addition happens before that
conversion, so an explicit count crashes for either default source:

```python
@click.command()
@click.option("-v", count=True, default="3")
def cli(v):
    click.echo(v)

runner.invoke(cli, []).output       # "3\n" (an int in the callback)
runner.invoke(cli, ["-v"]).exception
# TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str
```

The same exception occurs with `default_map={"v": "3"}`. Both baselines are
still raw strings in `consume_value`, while the parser count is an `int`; normal
type conversion only runs later in `handle_parse_result`. Could the baseline be
converted through the option type before adding it, with coverage for string
values from both `default` and `default_map`?

comments.issue_title: Add `shtab` to third-party contrib list
comments.author: casperdcl
comments.body:
Under-the-hood, a `click.Command` is turned into a temporary `argparse` object purely as an intermediate step in creating a completion script. Routing via any stdlib (such as `argparse`) is an implementation detail and unworthy of mention IMO.

Click's completions are currently unusably slow for complex apps, and it's not always desirable to move everything to lazy imports purely to make click's completions faster.

Using `shtab.click` instead does indeed deliberately remove all side-effects of the completion scripts (though it's likely easy to auto-detect [`hasattr('shell_complete')`](https://click.palletsprojects.com/en/stable/shell-completion/#custom-type-completion) to retain dynamic completion support where appropriate, vis. https://github.com/tqdm/shtab/issues/255).

The speedup feels noticeable even with the simple examples in the table above.

comments.issue_title: Add `Option.get_help_spec` to extract the help's left part of an hidden option
comments.author: kdeldycke
comments.body:
> > This will allow better integration for help-enhancing tools wrapping Click like Cloup (cc @janluke)
> 
> Can you explain how this new method help us or how do you plan to use it? We already get `(left_col, right_col)` from `get_help_record`.

Ah. I apologize. I was a bit quick to invoke you.😅 I just had an old impression that this was something you would rely on but I conflated my use-case and yours. I should have tripled-checked it. 🙇

I need to be more precise: this PR allows me to extract the `left_col` even when the option is hidden (`self.hidden is True`). This is the exact application of a workaround I had to introspect all parameters of a CLI, including those who are hidden: https://github.com/kdeldycke/click-extra/blob/68868d4489b87dca8247b2d73fc731167265febe/click_extra/parameters.py#L593-L613

This allows me to print metadata about an option (in this particular case its invocation specifications), outside its help screen context, and so outside the decision of either printing it to the user or not. Because an option hidden from the help screen is still an option recognize by the CLI and still has an effect on it. This is useful to implement deprecated options or preview options you don't want to advertise to the user. Still, you might need to print its specification in deprecation warnings, logs or error messages. That's where this new method can be useful.

In Click Extra I need the option specs to produce [machine-readable specs in JSON, Markdown and Carapace](https://kdeldycke.github.io/click-extra/machine-readable.html), and [live introspection](https://kdeldycke.github.io/click-extra/wrap.html#restricting-columns) rendering of third-party Click CLI.

comments.issue_title: Require a parameter name to be a non-keyword Python identifier
comments.author: davidism
comments.body:
This needs to be targeted at 9.0 and listed high up in the changelog, the name normalization is a breaking change. Along with the keyword check I mention below, this could be significantly disruptive. We should probably issue a deprecation warning and accept names that are currently accepted, before applying the new rules.

It might be good for the `TypeError` to give explicit instructions: `Argument {decls} tried to use 'name' but it is not a valid Python identifier. Add a valid name to the parameter declaration.`

Overall I think the docs are a little _too_ verbose about this. Giving a few examples and linking to `isidentifier` should be enough.

You bring up a good point about keywords. I think the intention of this code was clear: to only accept names that can be used in signatures rather than `kwargs`. We can also check that the name isn't a keyword with https://docs.python.org/3/library/keyword.html. I bet `from` and `in` are pretty common option names though, perhaps this is not worth it?

comments.issue_title: More private utilities that need to be marked and public api deprecated
comments.author: sirosen
comments.body:
Should `open_file` and `safecall` be made private as well?

I'm looking at adapting `pip-tools` to handle v8.5.0 this morning, and we have (this all looks weird to me)...
```python
my_file = click.open_file(filename, "w+b", atomic=True, lazy=True)
assert my_file is not None
if isinstance(my_file, click.utils.LazyFile):
    ctx.call_on_close(click.utils.safecall(my_file.close_intelligently))
```

I don't see any reason that anyone outside of `click` should ever use `safecall`: it's trivial to write it yourself. `open_file` doesn't seem good to expose if its return type won't be exposed. It's hard to figure out how to use it correctly in this case.

(We do want `close_intelligently()` since the target filename could be `"-"`.)
